title: Jump Game
statement:
You're given a list `nums` where nums[i] is the farthest you can jump forward from index i (you may also jump any shorter distance, including 1). You start at index 0. Return `True` if you can reach the last index, and `False` otherwise.

A 0 means you can't move forward from that spot, so landing on one is a dead end unless you got past it earlier.

Constraints: 1 <= len(nums) <= 400; 0 <= nums[i] <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: Jump 1 step to index 1, then 2 steps to index 3 (skipping the 0), then 1 step to the end.
From indexes 0, 1 and 2 you can get no farther than index 2, and the 0 there traps you.
You already stand on the last index.

hints: Think about which indexes you can reach at all, rather than which path to take. What does the set of reachable indexes look like?
If you can reach index i, which indexes does that make reachable? Is the reachable set always a solid block starting at 0?
So one number may be enough to describe it. What is the single most useful thing to remember as you scan left to right?
Try [3, 2, 1, 0, 4] and [2, 5, 0, 0]. When exactly is a 0 a trap, and when can you hop over it?
Track the farthest index reachable so far, update it at each index you can reach, and fail if you ever stand beyond it.
followUps: What are the time and space complexity of your solution, and what did a recursive or table approach cost by comparison?
Why is it enough to track only the farthest reachable index instead of exploring individual paths?
How would you return the minimum number of jumps needed to reach the end?
What if you could also jump backwards by the same amount?
How would you return an actual sequence of jumps that reaches the end?
idealAnswerPoints: Recognises that the reachable indexes always form a contiguous block starting at 0
Tracks the farthest reachable index in one left-to-right pass
Fails as soon as the current index is beyond the farthest reachable
Explains why a 0 is only fatal when it is the farthest reachable position
States O(n) time and O(1) space, and contrasts with exponential recursion or an O(n^2) table
weakAnswerSigns: Tries every jump length recursively with no memoisation, which times out on a few hundred elements
Returns False whenever it sees any 0 in the list
Only jumps the maximum distance each time, which can skip over the end or a better spot

rubric.correctness: Right answer on every test, including a single element, zeros that can be hopped over, and zeros that form a wall.
rubric.efficiency: Single pass, O(n) time and O(1) space. O(n^2) dynamic programming is only acceptable if named as a stepping stone.
rubric.code_quality: One variable for the farthest reach, a clear early exit, and no unnecessary data structures.
rubric.communication: Explains why the reachable set is contiguous before writing code.
